pdf_filename: Learning About the Past Through Digital Play History Students and Video Games.pdf

bibliographic.title: Learning About the Past Through Digital Play: History Students and Video Games
bibliographic.venue: Handbook of Digital Public History (De Gruyter)

study_characteristics.sample_description: Over 200 history students who responded to a survey about their perceptions of learning about history through playing video games; respondents were self-selecting student gamers
study_characteristics.study_design: qualitative survey with speculative design fiction
study_characteristics.game_type: commercial historical video games (various genres including strategy, RPG, action-adventure)
study_characteristics.game_name: Various (Assassin's Creed series mentioned prominently; also strategy games set in medieval periods)
study_characteristics.aim: To examine history students' perceptions of their learning about the past through playing video games, and to understand students' roles as active agents in learning about the past through virtual play rather than as passive consumers of digital products

eligibility.concerns: The study focuses on informal/leisure gameplay of commercial historical video games rather than formal classroom gamification interventions; it is a survey-based qualitative study about perceptions of learning rather than a controlled experiment measuring learning outcomes

rq1.conceptualization: The study does not provide an explicit definition of gamification. Instead, it conceptualizes the use of historical video games as a form of digital play through which students learn about history. The authors frame historical gaming as active engagement with the past through ludic structures, narrative, and agency within simulated historical environments. They also describe a university module (MD 348211 - Playing the Past: making history in digital spaces 01) that incorporates historical game-based learning including RPG elements, strategy gameplay, VR, game design/modding, and collaborative play.
theoretical_frameworks: Player agency and subjectivity in digital games (Charles 2009)
Historical game accuracy and authenticity (Copplestone 2017; Stirling and Wood 2021)
Self-Determination Theory / motivational model of video game engagement (Przybylski, Rigby, and Ryan 2010)
Speculative design fiction / design fiction prototyping (Sterling; Dunne and Raby 2013)
Narrative approaches to qualitative data analysis (Atkinson and Delamont 2005; Clandinin and Connelly 2000; Bold 2011)

rq2.quantitative_metrics: Table 2.1 presents frequency data from survey responses (n=213): Learn something (154), Try to find out more (148), Play another game (124), Talk to someone (93), Change the way you play the game (85), Visit a forum (47), Visit a place (43), Other (10). Follow-up on how gamers tried to find out more: online research (149), books (87), Wikipedia (86). 40% of respondents said they changed the way they played the game.
rq2.key_outcomes: Students perceived historical video games as powerful tools for learning about history. Key findings: (1) Motivation - students reported intrinsic motivation through agency, empowerment, and immersion in historical settings; interest in specific historical periods was sparked or deepened. (2) Experience - aesthetics, social interaction, choice/agency, and challenge were vital factors for positive gaming experience; games encouraged collaborative and social learning. (3) Learning - students reported learning historical information, engaging in historical/counterfactual thinking, understanding systemic contexts, and being motivated to conduct additional research outside the game. Gameplay extended beyond information acquisition to engagement in processes of historical thinking.
rq2.engagement_results: Students reported high engagement through: sense of agency and empowerment ('The plot arc gives a real sense of empowerment'), deep engagement with historical characters/polities, immersion in authentic historical environments, social/collaborative gameplay, replay value through different historical scenarios, and motivation to research topics beyond the game world (online research, books, Wikipedia, visiting places)

game_design_elements: Player agency and choice in historical scenarios
Historical accuracy and authenticity in game environments
Narrative and storyline set in historical periods
technological_platforms: VR rooms (mentioned in context of university module)
instructional_strategies: Speculative design fiction as pedagogical framing
University module combining gameplay with reflective learning (learning diaries, blog posts, quick voice memos)
Encouraging students to research historical topics beyond the game
Assessment based on engagement and reflection rather than traditional exams
Using student survey responses to inform module design
rq3.content_integration: Historical content is integrated through authentic historical settings, characters, events, and processes embedded within game narratives and mechanics. Games simulate historical environments (e.g., medieval Italy, Ancient Rome) allowing students to experience and interact with historical contexts. The university module described uses a week-long gameplay experience across different game types (first-person, strategy, collaborative) combined with reflective writing and game design activities. Students engage with historical content through active play, decision-making within historical scenarios, and counterfactual exploration.

implementation_barriers: Self-selecting sample - respondents were already enthusiastic gamers and positive about gaming
Student perception that gaming modules are not 'proper' History
Limited capacity on module (cap of 40 students)
Tension between games as entertainment vs. educational tools
Games create an 'illusion of agency' rather than true historical understanding
Historical accuracy concerns - games are 'not very accurate' representations of the past
Pathways in games are often restricted and can reinforce established or hegemonic interpretations
Need for institutional support (e.g., 24-hour learning center access, VR equipment, game engine partnerships)
methodology_limitations: Self-selecting survey sample leads to overwhelmingly positive responses about gaming
No control group or comparative condition
No direct measurement of actual learning outcomes - relies on self-reported perceptions
The speculative design fiction methodology is exploratory and generative rather than conclusive
Fiction was 80% participant voices and 20% narrative voice, introducing authorial interpretation
Study focuses on perceptions rather than objectively measured knowledge gains
negative_effects: Risk of reinforcing colonialist and hegemonic ideologies through game narratives
Games can direct gamers toward specific interpretations of the past, particularly in strategy games
Potential for games to create illusion of agency rather than genuine historical understanding
Some students may view gaming modules as not academically rigorous
mitigation_strategies: Using speculative design fiction to imagine alternative futures for history education
Combining gameplay with reflective activities (learning journals, voice memos, blog posts)
Including game design/modding to develop critical understanding of game construction
Incorporating multiple game types and collaborative activities
Drawing on user-centered approaches to understand student perspectives
Assessment designed around engagement and reflection

domain1.q1_evidence: The study uses a self-selecting convenience sample of student gamers who chose to respond to the survey. The authors explicitly acknowledge that 'respondents to our survey were self-selecting and, as such, were unsurprisingly positive about the experience of playing video games.' No formal inclusion/exclusion criteria for participants are described beyond being history students who play video games.
domain1.q2_evidence: The sample of 213 respondents represents only students who are already enthusiastic gamers. The authors acknowledge this limitation. The sample is drawn from a single university context in the UK, limiting representativeness. No demographic breakdown is provided beyond being history students.

domain2.q3_evidence: The survey instrument is not described in detail. The study mentions survey questions with predefined response options (Table 2.1) and free-text responses, but no information is provided about instrument validation, piloting, or reliability. The speculative design fiction approach is a creative methodology but lacks standardized evaluation criteria.
domain2.q4_evidence: The authors describe their thematic analysis approach: they separately coded the dataset, identified themes, came together to review and cross-check codes and emerging themes, and extracted representative quotes. They were transparent about the fiction being 80% participant voices and 20% narrative voice. The analytical approach follows established qualitative methods (Atkinson and Delamont; Clandinin and Connelly).

domain3.q5_evidence: The findings are consistently presented across three themes (motivation, experience, learning) that align with the research aims. Survey data (Table 2.1) and qualitative quotes support the interpretations made. The speculative design fiction is clearly distinguished from the analytical discussion.
domain3.q6_evidence: The authors explicitly acknowledge the self-selecting nature of their sample and the overwhelmingly positive responses this produced. They discuss the paradox of gamers being 'tightly constrained in their ability to experience the past' while still finding gaming valuable. Limitations of the speculative design fiction approach are partially acknowledged through its framing as exploratory and generative.

risk_of_bias.overall_justification: While the qualitative analysis and interpretation are conducted with reasonable methodological rigor, the study has significant limitations in its sampling approach (self-selecting enthusiastic gamers), lack of validated instruments, absence of direct learning outcome measurement, and limited generalizability from a single UK university context. The speculative design fiction methodology is innovative but makes it difficult to separate empirical findings from creative interpretation. The study provides valuable qualitative insights into student perceptions but cannot support strong causal claims about the effectiveness of historical video games for learning.
